arXiv:2604.12281v1 [cs.CV] 14 Apr 2026

MAST: Mask-Guided Attention Mass Allocation for
Training-Free Multi-Style Transfer

Dongkyung Kang*, Jaeyeon Hwang*, Junseo Park*, Minji Kang*, Yeryeong Lee*, Beomseok Ko, Hanyoung Roh, Jeongmin Shin, Hyeryung Jang† Affiliation: Division of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Dongguk University, Republic of Korea
Abstract.

Style transfer aims to render a content image with the visual characteristics of a reference style while preserving its underlying semantic layout and structural geometry. While recent diffusion-based models demonstrate strong stylization capabilities by leveraging powerful generative priors and controllable internal representations, they typically assume a single global style. Extending them to multi-style scenarios often leads to boundary artifacts, unstable stylization, and structural inconsistency due to interference between multiple style representations. To overcome these limitations, we propose MAST (Mask-Guided Attention Mass Allocation for Training-Free Multi-Style Transfer), a novel training-free framework that explicitly controls content-style interactions within the diffusion attention mechanism. To achieve artifact-free and structure-preserving stylization, MAST integrates four connected modules. First, Layout-preserving Query Anchoring prevents global layout collapse by firmly anchoring the semantic structure using content queries. Second, Logit-level Attention Mass Allocation deterministically distributes attention probability mass across spatial regions, seamlessly fusing multiple styles without boundary artifacts. Third, Sharpness-aware Temperature Scaling restores the attention sharpness degraded by multi-style expansion. Finally, Discrepancy-aware Detail Injection adaptively compensates for localized high-frequency detail losses by measuring structural discrepancies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MAST effectively mitigates boundary artifacts and maintains structural consistency, preserving texture fidelity and spatial coherence even as the number of applied styles increases.

1. Introduction

Image style transfer aims to render a content image with the visual characteristics of a reference style while preserving its underlying semantic layout and structural geometry. This task has long been a core challenge in computer vision and graphics, with applications ranging from artistic image generation to creative production (Dumoulin et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017; Lei et al., 2025a). Early methods (Gatys et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2022) primarily relied on CNN-based optimization or global statistical matching. To improve efficiency and capture long-range dependencies, subsequent works (Deng et al., 2022; Zuo et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024) adopted GAN and Transformer architectures. Despite their progress, these non-diffusion approaches often rely on global feature statistics, which fail to capture fine-grained local structures and frequently lead to shape distortions or texture leakage across object boundaries.

To overcome these limitations, diffusion-based models (Deng et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025) have emerged as a superior paradigm, leveraging strong generative priors and controllable internal representations to achieve high-fidelity stylization. However, most existing diffusion frameworks (Zhang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024b) are inherently designed for single-style transfer, assuming a uniform global style for the entire image. As the demand for more granular control grows, such as applying distinct stylistic intentions to specific objects within a single scene, extending these models to multi-style scenarios becomes essential.

The primary technical obstacle in multi-style expansion is the interference between multiple style representations within the diffusion attention mechanism. Since the internal attention process is inherently global, style information intended for one masked region via naive pixel-level masking often leaks into unintended areas, causing unwanted blending and visual noise. Furthermore, as the model attempts to incorporate multiple style references simultaneously, its focus becomes weakened - a phenomenon we define as “attention flattening”. This dilution of stylistic focus prevents the model from capturing the vivid textures of each intended style, leading to blurred textures and abrupt statistical discontinuities at mask boundaries, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

To address these limitations, we propose MAST (Mask-Guided Attention Mass Allocation for Training-Free Multi-Style Transfer), a novel framework designed to disentangle spatial style control from content preservation by regulating how stylistic resources are distributed in the diffusion attention mechanism. Unlike previous methods that struggle to block internal style leakage, MAST achieves precise multi-style fusion at the logit level through the following technical pillars:

  • •

    Logit-level Attention Mass Allocation (LAMA): To eliminate style conflict, LAMA deterministically rescales the distribution of stylistic resources, i.e., attention probability mass, at the network’s logit level. By satisfying the probability-mass conservation principle, it ensures that each style is injected precisely into its designated region, preventing leakage and ensuring artifact-free transitions.

  • •

    Sharpness-aware Temperature Scaling (STS): To counteract attention flattening, STS acts as an active focus recovery mechanism. It adaptively restores the model’s confidence by sharpening the internal attention distribution, enabling the vivid rendering of distinct stylistic textures even in complex multi-style scenarios.

  • •

    Dual-scale structural preservation (LQA and DDI): We employ a two-tiered strategy to protect content integrity at both global and local scales. Layout-preserving Query Anchoring (LQA) acts as a global anchor to stabilize the overall semantic structure, while Discrepancy-aware Detail Injection (DDI) restores fine textures and sharp edges by selectively compensating for structural discrepancies identified in the frequency domain.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that MAST produces state-of-the-art results, maintaining high texture fidelity and spatial coherence even as the number of applied styles increases. In summary, our key contributions are: (i) a unified training-free framework for multi-style transfer; (ii) a deterministic logit-level style allocation via LAMA to prevent inter-style interference; (iii) the STS mechanism for restoring stylistic clarity and focus; and (iv) a dual-scale content preservation strategy, i.e., LQA and DDI, to robustly maintain structural fidelity against strong stylistic injections.

2. Related work

Image Style Transfer. Early CNN-based methods (Gatys et al., 2016) utilized perceptual features and global statistics, often failing to capture fine-grained style details or achieve proper disentanglement. Subsequent GAN- (Zuo et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024) and Transformer-based (Deng et al., 2022; Park and Kim, 2022; Wang et al., 2022) approaches improved efficiency and long-range dependency modeling. They enable flexible and precise stylization with real-time and multi-modal control, as well as complex semantics. However, these methods frequently struggle with structural preservation and precise style control, motivating the rise of diffusion-based alternatives as a more stable paradigm.

Diffusion-based Style Transfer. Diffusion models offer superior stylization quality, categorized into training-based and training-free approaches. Training-based methods (Chen et al., 2025; Chigot et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025) fine-tune models on content–style pairs to improve consistency and controllability. In contrast, training-free methods manipulate internal representations - such as attention maps or latent features - to enable flexible stylization without additional training (Deng et al., 2024; Chung et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2024; Jeong et al., 2023; Lei et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). Image-guided techniques refine the process through attention reweighting, e.g., StyleID (Chung et al., 2024) and Z∗Z^{*} (Deng et al., 2024), or content-aware normalization (Huang et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2024; Jeong et al., 2023), while prompt-driven methods guide stylization via cross-model alignment or textual inversion (Lei et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023).

Despite their flexibility, existing diffusion-based methods are primarily designed for single-style transfer and lack explicit mechanisms for handling multiple styles across spatial regions. This often results in interference and artifacts when multiple styles are introduced. Our approach is a training-free framework that explicitly addresses mask-based multi-style transfer through deterministic attention mass allocation.

3. Preliminaries

3.1. Latent Diffusion Models

Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) (Rombach et al., 2022) perform the denoising process in the latent space of an autoencoder. Given a fixed encoder ℰ\mathcal{E}, an input image xx is mapped to a latent representation z0=ℰ⁡(x)z_{0}=\mathcal{E}(x). The forward diffusion process is defined as zt=α¯t​z0+1−α¯t​ϵz_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}z_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\epsilon, where ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) and α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} is a time-dependent scaling factor. The denoising network ϵθ​(zt,t,y)\epsilon_{\theta}(z_{t},t,y) is trained to predict the added noise at each timestep tt, optionally conditioned on yy (e.g., text, image). The training objective is:

(1) ℒLDM=𝔼z,ϵ,t​[‖ϵ−ϵθ​(zt,t,y)‖22].\mathcal{L}_{\text{LDM}}=\mathbb{E}_{z,\epsilon,t}\left[\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}(z_{t},t,y)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right].

3.2. Style Transfer with Diffusion Attention

Latent diffusion models are typically implemented with U-Net architectures that incorporate attention modules to model spatial dependencies. In particular, self-attention mechanisms capture long-range interactions within feature maps. Given query, key, and value features QQ, KK, and VV, the attention operation is defined as:

(2) Attention​(ℓ,V)=Softmax​(ℓ)​V,ℓ=Q​K⊤d,\text{Attention}(\ell,V)=\text{Softmax}(\ell)V,\quad\ell=\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}},

where ℓ\ell denotes the attention logits.

In diffusion-based style transfer, three feature paths are typically considered: the content path cc, the style path ss, and the stylized path c​scs. The content path preserves structural and semantic information, while the style path provides stylistic attributes such as texture and color, and the stylized path represents the generation process where style is integrated into content. Using DDIM (Song et al., 2020) inversion, self-attention feature maps are extracted from both content and style images and injected into the stylized path at each timestep, enabling controllable stylization while preserving content structure.

4. Methodology

We propose MAST, a training-free framework for mask-based multi-style transfer. Given a content image IcI_{c} and NN style-mask pairs {(Is(i),M(i))}i=1N\{(I_{s}^{(i)},M^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{N}, our goal is to synthesize a stylized image Ic​sI_{cs} that precisely applies localized styles while preserving the global semantic layout. Building on the paradigm of attention-based stylization (Deng et al., 2024; Chung et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024b; Alaluf et al., 2024), we manipulate self-attention features from DDIM inversion to inject stylistic attributes.

As illustrated in Fig. 2, our framework operates on three paths: the content path (zTcz_{T}^{c} inverted from IcI_{c}), the style paths (zTs,(i)z_{T}^{s,(i)} from each Is(i)I_{s}^{(i)}), and the stylization path starting from zTc​sz_{T}^{cs}. To ensure color fidelity, we initialize the stylization latent zTc​sz_{T}^{cs} by applying region-wise AdaIN (Huang and Belongie, 2017) to zTcz_{T}^{c} using the channel statistics of each style image:

(3) zTc​s=∑i=1NM(i)⊙AdaIN⁡(zTc,zTs,(i))+(1−∑i=1NM(i))⊙zTcz_{T}^{cs}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}M^{(i)}\odot\mathrm{AdaIN}(z_{T}^{c},z_{T}^{s,(i)})+\left(1-\sum_{i=1}^{N}M^{(i)}\right)\odot z_{T}^{c}

Following this initialization, style is injected during the denoising process through our core attention control modules.

4.1. Layout-preserving Query Anchoring

To preserve the semantic layout of IcI_{c} during style injection, we employ LQA. While replacing self-attention keys and values (K,V)(K,V) with style features (Ks,Vs)(K_{s},V_{s}) facilitates stylization, the query Qc​sQ_{cs} often lacks sufficient structural priors, leading to layout collapse. Since the query governs the spatial distribution of attention, anchoring it with QcQ_{c} ensures that style tokens are accurately mapped to the original semantic regions. To this end, we blend the queries Qc​sQ_{cs} and QcQ_{c} as follows:

(4) Q^c​s=λ⋅Qc+(1−λ)⋅Qc​s,\hat{Q}_{cs}=\lambda\cdot Q_{c}+(1-\lambda)\cdot Q_{cs},

where λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] modulates the structural guidance from the content path. We empirically set λ=0.2\lambda=0.2 to balance structural fidelity and stylization quality. As illustrated in Fig. 3, omitting LQA (i.e., λ=0\lambda=0) results in severe structural degradation, whereas Q^c​s\hat{Q}_{cs} in (4) effectively stabilizes the spatial configuration while allowing for stylistic transformation.

4.2. Logit-level Attention Mass Allocation

We propose LAMA (Logit-level Attention Mass Allocation) to deterministically regulate stylization strength at the logit level. By enforcing a target style attention mass π∗\pi^{*}, LAMA achieves precise spatial control while preserving content integrity. For a given (continuous) mask M∈[0,1]M\in[0,1], we define the location-dependent attention mass as πc​s∗=π∗⋅M\pi_{cs}^{*}=\pi^{*}\cdot M. Unlike conventional attention masking, LAMA enforces a hard constraint on the total attention mass, effectively preventing stylistic leakage into unintended regions and facilitating seamless boundary transitions (see Fig. 4).

Specifically, we concatenate the style and content logits, ℓc​o​n​c​a​t=[ℓc​s,ℓc]\ell_{concat}=[\ell_{cs},\;\ell_{c}], to separate tokens into distinct groups. To satisfy the target mass distribution while preserving the relative ranking within each group, we introduce a learnable-free bias bb to the style logits (see Appendix A.1 for details):

(5) ℓc​o​n​c​a​t=[ℓc​s+b,ℓc].\ell_{concat}=[\ell_{cs}+b,\;\ell_{c}].

The bias bb is computed through a closed-form derivation to ensure the total attention mass satisfies (πc​s∗,πc∗)=(π∗⋅M, 1−π∗⋅M)(\pi_{cs}^{*},\pi_{c}^{*})=(\pi^{*}\cdot M,\;1-\pi^{*}\cdot M). We empirically set π∗=0.9\pi^{*}=0.9.

Our ultimate goal is to achieve multi-style transfer by seamlessly integrating multiple styles into a single image. LAMA naturally extends to mask-based multi-style transfer by deterministically allocating the per-region style proportion according to user-specified ratios. Given NN styles with corresponding masks {M(i)}i=1N\{M^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}, we define:

(6) πc​s∗,(i)=π∗⋅M(i),πc∗=1−∑i=1Nπc​s∗,(i),\pi_{cs}^{*,(i)}=\pi^{*}\cdot M^{(i)},\quad\pi_{c}^{*}=1-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\pi_{cs}^{*,(i)},

ensuring ∑iπc​s∗,(i)+πc∗=1\sum_{i}\pi_{cs}^{*,(i)}+\pi_{c}^{*}=1. Each style is assigned a bias b(i)b^{(i)}, and the final logits are:

(7) ℓc​o​n​c​a​t=[ℓc​s(1)+b(1),…,ℓc​s(N)+b(N),ℓc].\ell_{concat}=[\ell_{cs}^{(1)}+b^{(1)},\dots,\ell_{cs}^{(N)}+b^{(N)},\ell_{c}].

4.3. Sharpness-aware Temperature Scaling

We address the degradation of attention sharpness by introducing STS (Sharpness-aware Temperature Scaling). While LAMA enables mask-based multi-style transfer, it leads to a flattened attention distribution, suppressing dominant tokens and degrading stylization and structural patterns.

This issue arises from two factors. First, the similarity in ℓc​s(i)\ell_{cs}^{(i)} becomes flattened due to low correlation between Q^c​s\hat{Q}_{cs} and Ks(i)K_{s}^{(i)}, reducing logit variance. Second, concatenating ℓc​s(i)\ell_{cs}^{(i)} and ℓc\ell_{c} increases the number of tokens, enlarging the softmax normalization term and reducing logit contrast, as observed in prior work (Veličković et al., 2024).

To address this, we apply temperature scaling τ\tau to the attention logits. Unlike StyleID (Chung et al., 2024) using a fixed τ\tau, we adapt it per sample using content–content logits ℓc\ell_{c} as a reference. We measure sharpness via log⁡pm​a​x\log p_{max} and define the gap (see Appendix A.2):

(8) Δ=log⁡pm​a​x​(ℓc)−log⁡pm​a​x​(ℓc​o​n​c​a​t)\Delta=\log p_{max}(\ell_{c})-\log p_{max}(\ell_{concat})

As shown in Fig. 5a, Δ\Delta exhibits a monotonic relationship with temperature. Based on this, we approximate τ=f⁡(Δ)\tau=f(\Delta) using a polynomial fit and compute the attention output as

(9) Attention​(τ​ℓc​o​n​c​a​t,Vc​o​n​c​a​t)=Softmax​(τ​ℓc​o​n​c​a​t)​Vc​o​n​c​a​t,\text{Attention}(\tau\ell_{concat},V_{concat})=\text{Softmax}(\tau\ell_{concat})V_{concat},

where Vc​o​n​c​a​t=[Vs(1),…,Vs(N),Vc]V_{concat}=[V_{s}^{(1)},\dots,V_{s}^{(N)},V_{c}]. STS restores attention sharpness and improves confidence (Fig. 5b). Overall, attention control is achieved through two complementary mechanisms: LAMA governs global attention allocation, while STS refines the distribution locally.

4.4. Discrepancy-aware Detail Injection

We introduce DDI (Discrepancy-aware Detail Injection), a high-frequency enhancement module to preserve fine details lost during stylization. While LQA maintains the overall layout and LAMA partially preserves the probability mass of content tokens, both under-emphasize content, leading to the loss of high-frequency details such as textures, edges, and fine structures (e.g., eyes and hair).

To address this, following prior residual-based approaches (Hu et al., 2024b; Lei et al., 2025b), we extract high-frequency components ϕchigh\phi_{c}^{\text{high}} from the content feature using a Gaussian high-pass filter with radius rr in the frequency domain (see Appendix A.3). Let ϕc\phi_{c} and ϕc​s\phi_{cs} denote the residual block outputs of the content and stylized paths, respectively, and Δ​ϕc​s\Delta\phi_{cs} the residual in the stylized path.

We modulate the injection of ϕchigh\phi_{c}^{\text{high}} based on the structural discrepancy between ϕc​s\phi_{cs} and ϕc\phi_{c}. Specifically, we define a cosine-based weight ω=1−cos⁡(ϕc​s,ϕc)\omega=1-\cos(\phi_{cs},\phi_{c}), which increases with the discrepancy. The final output is:

(10) ϕ^c​s=ϕc​s+Δ​ϕc​s+ω⋅ϕchigh\hat{\phi}_{cs}=\phi_{cs}+\Delta\phi_{cs}+\omega\cdot\phi_{c}^{\text{high}}

This enhances high-frequency details when structural distortion is large and suppresses it otherwise, preserving fine structures while maintaining stylistic consistency.

5. Experiment

Datasets. We construct content–style pairs by randomly sampling 2020 content images from MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014) and 360360 style images from WikiArt (WikiArt, 2026), resulting in diverse combinations spanning various scene layouts and artistic styles. The total number of evaluation samples depends on the number of masked regions NN, yielding 7,200/N7{,}200/N images.

Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate style transfer in terms of both content preservation and style fidelity using complementary metrics: FID, LPIPS, LPIPS-Gray, CFSD, and their combined metric, ArtFID. ArtFID is used as the primary metric, as it jointly captures content and style quality and correlates well with human perception: ArtFID=(1+LPIPS)⋅(1+FID)\text{ArtFID}=(1+\text{LPIPS})\cdot(1+\text{FID}). FID measures the distributional similarity between generated and style images, reflecting style fidelity. LPIPS evaluates perceptual similarity to the content image, measuring content preservation. LPIPS-Gray removes color information to focus on structural consistency. CFSD measures structural consistency via spatial feature correlations, reducing sensitivity to style-induced textures. Additionally, for mask-based multi-style transfer, we introduce Masked FID (M-FID) to evaluate stylization within specific regions. We restrict feature aggregation to masked areas and compute FID only over the stylized regions.

Implementation details. All experiments are conducted using Stable Diffusion v1.4 with DDIM sampling (50 steps). We set λ=0.2\lambda=0.2, π∗=0.9\pi^{*}=0.9 and r=0.3r=0.3. Our method operates on self-attention modules in the U-Net, applying feature manipulation at all timesteps to decoder layers 7–12, where high-level semantic interactions are dominant. Text prompts are set to null strings.

Baselines. We compare our method with several state-of-the-art style transfer and diffusion-based stylization methods, including StyTr2 (Deng et al., 2022), InST (Zhang et al., 2023), CAST (Zhang et al., 2022), Z∗Z^{*} (Deng et al., 2024), StyleID (Chung et al., 2024), DiffuseST (Hu et al., 2024b), StyleSSP (Xu et al., 2025), and StyleShot (Gao et al., 2025). For all baselines, we follow the official implementations from their publicly available repositories. Since most methods are designed for single-style transfer, we extend them to the multi-style setting using mask-based element-wise composition for fair comparison.

5.1. Evaluation in the Two-style Setting

Our method achieves the best overall performance in the two-style setting, demonstrating a strong balance between content preservation and stylization. As shown in Tab. 1, it outperforms all baselines in ArtFID, achieves the lowest FID, and obtains superior CFSD scores, indicating improved overall quality and strong structural and pattern consistency.

While Z∗Z^{*} (Deng et al., 2024), DiffuseST (Hu et al., 2024b), and StyleID (Chung et al., 2024) report competitive LPIPS and LPIPS-Gray, Fig. 6 shows that their low LPIPS largely results from limited perceptual changes, leading to insufficient stylization. In contrast, our method preserves structure while introducing meaningful style variations, achieving a better balance despite relatively higher LPIPS. It also achieves the best M-FID across regions, demonstrating accurate region-wise style alignment.

Qualitative comparisons in Fig. 6 highlight three key strengths: fine detail preservation, structural consistency, and smooth boundary transitions. In the first row, our method preserves fine details, such as the reflection on the toilet tank lid, while StyleSSP (Xu et al., 2025) and StyleShot (Gao et al., 2025) overemphasize style and degrade structural information. In the second row, our method maintains the geometric layout of the tiles while effectively transferring the background style, whereas all baselines, including Z∗Z^{*}, fail to capture the background style and distort structure and patterns.

In the third row, several baselines exhibit clear artifacts. StyleSSP and StyleShot introduce unrealistic distortions, while InST, Z∗Z^{*}, and DiffuseST fail to properly transfer the background style, resulting in inconsistent outputs. This issue persists in the fourth row, where Z∗Z^{*} and DiffuseST again fail to reflect the background style. Meanwhile, other methods apply the background style without respecting the foreground, causing visible discontinuities at mask boundaries. In contrast, our method suppresses structural distortions and artifacts while maintaining consistent stylization.

5.2. Multi-style Scalability

Our method demonstrates strong scalability, maintaining consistent performance and stable style composition as the number of styles increases. To qualitatively validate this, Fig. 7 presents results under a 5-style mask setting with sequential style addition. Even with narrow mask regions and increasing style complexity, styles are consistently applied across content and background while preserving object identity. Previously applied styles remain stable as new styles are introduced, with clear separation between foreground and background and no noticeable style leakage.

For example, even with strong style images (last two rows, with target spatial masks shown in orange and blue), no style interference is observed in adjacent content regions (e.g., the dog and pizza). At the same time, the distinctive visual characteristics of each style—such as the lighting in the ice castle and the vivid colors of the cat—are faithfully preserved.

For quantitative evaluation, we measure ArtFID while increasing the number of styles from 11 to 55, as shown in Fig. 8. Most baseline methods suffer significant performance degradation when transitioning from single-style to multi-style settings, with a sharp drop at the 1→21{\rightarrow}2 transition, as reflected in the violin plots, since they are not explicitly designed for mask-based multi-style transfer.

In contrast, our method improves performance from 1→21{\rightarrow}2 and remains stable thereafter, demonstrating effective style disentanglement and control. While methods such as Z∗Z^{*} and StyleID show relatively stable trends, they still underperform compared to ours. Quantitatively, our method achieves the lowest MAD across varying numbers of styles, indicating strong robustness as the number of styles increases.

5.3. Analysis of Multi-Style Interaction

In multi-style settings, unlike naive copy-and-paste approaches (see Fig. 1), styles are not applied independently but interact within the overall composition. In particular, changes in the background style directly affect the appearance of the character style in the 2-style setting. As shown in Fig. 9, each row keeps the same character style while varying only the background style. Even with an identical character style, its visual expression changes depending on the accompanying background, indicating that style appearance is determined by the global composition.

This behavior arises from our multi-style design and can be explained by the combined effects of LAMA and STS. LAMA processes multiple styles jointly with respect to a shared content anchor, rather than independently. Each style adjusts its relative influence in relation to others, so changes in one style affect the overall compositional balance, leading to coherent integration across styles.

Moreover, different style combinations produce different attention logit distributions, resulting in variations in log⁡pmax\log p_{\max}. Since τ\tau is determined based on log⁡pmax\log p_{\max}, each combination yields a different temperature. Consequently, STS adaptively modulates the sharpness of the attention distribution, causing even the same style to exhibit different visual characteristics.

Overall, our method enables adaptive variation in style expression while maintaining balanced integration, resulting in coherent multi-style compositions. This explains the strong scalability observed in Sec. 5.2.

5.4. Ablation Study

We conduct an ablation study by progressively adding each component to the initial setting, analyzing both individual contributions and their combined effects. To evaluate the effect of LQA, we first consider a single-style transfer setting without mask guidance. Since LAMA and STS are designed for mask-based multi-style transfer, they are evaluated under a two-style setting. The qualitative effects of each component are shown in Fig. 10.

As shown in Table. 2, introducing LQA improves LPIPS by better preserving content layout. However, without explicit control over style injection, the model exhibits strong content bias, resulting in limited stylization. Adding LAMA enables spatially selective style injection and controllable stylization strength, significantly improving ArtFID and FID. While stylization becomes more pronounced, some content details—such as the surface texture of the Statue of Liberty, signs, and foliage—are partially degraded.

Further improvements are achieved with STS, which sharpens the attention distribution and enhances stylization precision, mitigating blur caused by overly flat attention. Finally, incorporating DDI restores lost textures and improves fine detail preservation (e.g., text), leading to additional gains in LPIPS and CFSD. However, this comes with a slight trade-off, as ArtFID and FID degrade due to increased emphasis on content fidelity.

6. Conclusion

In this work, we presented MAST, a mask-based multi-style transfer framework that explicitly controls the interaction between content and multiple styles within the diffusion attention mechanism. By integrating LQA, LAMA, STS, and DDI, our method effectively disentangles content preservation and style control while addressing challenges such as boundary artifacts, attention degradation, and structural inconsistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MAST achieves superior performance across both quantitative and qualitative evaluations, providing accurate region-wise style alignment, strong structural and pattern consistency, and stable stylization even as the number of styles increases. Overall, our results highlight the importance of explicitly modeling content–style interactions for multi-style transfer and suggest a promising direction for scalable and controllable image generation.

Appendix A Research Methods

A.1. Mathematical Formulation of LAMA

In this section, we present the mathematical formulation of LAMA (Logit-level Attention Mass Allocation), parameterized by π∗\pi^{*}, for mask-based style transfer. We then derive the corresponding closed-form solution for injecting it into the attention map.

A.1.1. Definition of probability mass in single-style attention

In the single-style setting, let ℓc​s​(q)∈ℝTc​s\ell_{cs}(q)\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{cs}} and ℓc​(q)∈ℝTc\ell_{c}(q)\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{c}} denote the style and content logit vectors for a query token qq. We define the concatenated logit vector as

(11) ℓconcat​(q)=[ℓc​s​(q),ℓc​(q)]∈ℝTc​s+Tc.\ell_{\mathrm{concat}}(q)=[\,\ell_{cs}(q),\;\ell_{c}(q)\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{cs}+T_{c}}.

Applying a single Softmax to ℓconcat​(q)\ell_{\mathrm{concat}}(q) induces a probability distribution over both style and content tokens. Accordingly, the style and content partition functions are defined as

(12) Zc​s(q)=∑j=1Tc​sexp(ℓconcat(q,j)),Zc(q)=∑j=Tc​s+1Tc​s+Tcexp(ℓconcat(q,j)),Ztotal​(q)=Zc​s​(q)+Zc​(q).\begin{gathered}Z_{cs}(q)=\sum_{j=1}^{T_{cs}}\exp\!\big(\ell_{\mathrm{concat}}(q,j)\big),\;Z_{c}(q)=\sum_{j=T_{cs}+1}^{T_{cs}+T_{c}}\exp\!\big(\ell_{\mathrm{concat}}(q,j)\big),\\ Z_{\mathrm{total}}(q)=Z_{cs}(q)+Z_{c}(q).\end{gathered}

The corresponding probability masses assigned to the style and content partitions are then given by

(13) πc​s​(q)=Zc​s​(q)Ztotal​(q),πc​(q)=Zc​(q)Ztotal​(q),\pi_{cs}(q)=\frac{Z_{cs}(q)}{Z_{\mathrm{total}}(q)},\qquad\pi_{c}(q)=\frac{Z_{c}(q)}{Z_{\mathrm{total}}(q)},

with πc​s​(q)+πc​(q)=1\pi_{cs}(q)+\pi_{c}(q)=1.

A.1.2. Target mass allocation for single-style by LAMA

Assume that a spatial mask M⁡(q)∈[0,1]M(q)\in[0,1] is given for query token qq to specify where style is injected. Let π∗\pi^{*} denote the maximum fraction of the total attention mass allocated to the style partition. The target probability masses for the style and content partitions are then defined as

(14) πc​s∗​(q)=π∗⋅M⁡(q),πc∗​(q)=1−π∗⋅M⁡(q).\pi_{cs}^{*}(q)=\pi^{*}\cdot M(q),\quad\pi_{c}^{*}(q)=1-\pi^{*}\cdot M(q).

When M⁡(q)=1M(q)=1, the full target style mass π∗\pi^{*} is assigned to the style partition. When M⁡(q)=0M(q)=0, πc​s∗​(q)=0\pi_{cs}^{*}(q)=0, so no attention mass is allocated to style and the content is fully preserved.

A.1.3. Closed-form solution for single-style injection

To match the style probability mass to the target value πc​s∗​(q)\pi_{cs}^{*}(q), we add a shared bias b⁡(q)b(q) to all style logits:

(15) ℓconcat​(q)=[ℓc​s​(q)+b⁡(q),ℓc​(q)].\ell_{\mathrm{concat}}(q)=[\,\ell_{cs}(q)+b(q),\;\ell_{c}(q)\,].

Under this biased concatenation, the probability mass assigned to the style partition becomes

(16) exp⁡(b⁡(q))​Zc​s​(q)exp⁡(b⁡(q))​Zc​s​(q)+Zc​(q)=πc​s∗​(q).\frac{\exp(b(q))\,Z_{cs}(q)}{\exp(b(q))\,Z_{cs}(q)+Z_{c}(q)}=\pi_{cs}^{*}(q).

Solving this equation for b⁡(q)b(q) yields the closed-form solution

(17) b⁡(q)=log⁡(πc​s∗​(q)πc∗​(q))+log⁡Zc​(q)−log⁡Zc​s​(q).b(q)=\log\!\left(\frac{\pi_{cs}^{*}(q)}{\pi_{c}^{*}(q)}\right)+\log Z_{c}(q)-\log Z_{cs}(q).

This bias exactly matches the target style mass while preserving the relative ordering within ℓc​s​(q)\ell_{cs}(q).

A.1.4. Generalization to NN-way multi-style injection.

The single-style formulation of LAMA naturally extends to the multi-style setting with NN style partitions. For a query token qq, let ℓc​s(i)​(q)\ell_{cs}^{(i)}(q) denote the logit vector of the ii-th style partition for i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N. The total partition function is then defined as

(18) Ztotal​(q)=Zc​(q)+∑i=1NZc​s(i)​(q).Z_{\mathrm{total}}(q)=Z_{c}(q)+\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{cs}^{(i)}(q).

The target probability mass for each style partition is defined as

(19) πc​s∗,(i)​(q)=π∗⋅M(i)​(q),πc∗​(q)=1−∑i=1Nπc​s∗,(i)​(q).\pi_{cs}^{*,(i)}(q)=\pi^{*}\cdot M^{(i)}(q),\qquad\pi_{c}^{*}(q)=1-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\pi_{cs}^{*,(i)}(q).

To match the target mass of each style partition, we add an independent bias b(i)​(q)b^{(i)}(q) to each style logit group. The concatenated logits are then written as

(20) ℓconcat​(q)=[ℓc​s(1)​(q)+b(1)​(q),…,ℓc​s(N)​(q)+b(N)​(q),ℓc​(q)].\ell_{\mathrm{concat}}(q)=\big[\ell_{cs}^{(1)}(q)+b^{(1)}(q),\;\dots,\;\ell_{cs}^{(N)}(q)+b^{(N)}(q),\;\ell_{c}(q)\big].

This formulation reduces to the single-style case when N=1N=1. Moreover, the target masses satisfy

(21) ∑i=1Nπc​s∗,(i)​(q)+πc∗​(q)=1,\sum_{i=1}^{N}\pi_{cs}^{*,(i)}(q)+\pi_{c}^{*}(q)=1,

which ensures conservation of the total probability mass regardless of the number of styles.

A.1.5. Selection of π∗\pi^{*}

We quantitatively evaluate different values of π∗\pi^{*} in the two-style setting, as shown in Table 3, to identify the best balance between generative quality and structural fidelity. The results reveal a clear trade-off. Lower π∗\pi^{*} values (e.g., 0.30.3–0.60.6) yield better perceptual similarity and structural alignment, as shown by lower LPIPS, LPIPS-Gray, and CFSD scores, but at the cost of worse image generation quality, reflected in higher ArtFID, FID and M-FID scores.

We choose π∗=0.9\pi^{*}=0.9 as the default setting because it achieves the best overall generative performance, yielding the lowest ArtFID (14.780), FID (8.656) and M-FID (15.193) among all tested values. By contrast, π∗=1.0\pi^{*}=1.0 degrades both generative quality and perceptual distance metrics. Thus, π∗=0.9\pi^{*}=0.9 provides the best balance between image quality and structural consistency.

A.2. Sharpness-aware Temperature Scaling

We provide theoretical and empirical analyses of STS (Sharpness-aware Temperature Scaling), including the derivation of the (Δ\Delta, τ\tau) relationship and the construction of the mapping function τ=f⁡(Δ)\tau=f(\Delta). Although the optimal temperature depends on the full attention logit distribution, we find that the sharpness gap Δ\Delta explains most of the variance in the optimal temperature τ∗\tau^{*} (R2≈0.93R^{2}\approx 0.93 in Table 4). This suggests that τ\tau can be effectively approximated as a function of Δ\Delta without access to the full distribution.

A.2.1. Monotonic Relationship Between log⁡pmax\log p_{\max} and τ\tau

For a query token qq, let ℓc​(q)\ell_{c}(q) denote the content logits, and let ℓconcat​(q)\ell_{\text{concat}}(q) denote the concatenated logits defined in Eq. (20). We define the sharpness gap as

(22) Δ=log⁡pmax​(ℓc)−log⁡pmax​(ℓconcat),\Delta=\log p_{\max}(\ell_{c})-\log p_{\max}(\ell_{\text{concat}}),

where pmax​(ℓ)p_{\max}(\ell) denotes the maximum softmax probability computed from logits ℓ\ell. Thus, Δ\Delta quantifies the loss of attention sharpness caused by logit concatenation. To compensate for this loss, we scale ℓconcat\ell_{\text{concat}} by a temperature τ\tau, i.e., τ​ℓconcat\tau\ell_{\text{concat}}.

Let ℓ⁡(q)∈ℝT\ell(q)\in\mathbb{R}^{T} be the pre-softmax attention logits over TT tokens, and let ℓmax​(q)\ell_{\max}(q) be the maximum logit. Under temperature scaling,

(23) logpmax(τℓ(q))=logeτ​ℓmax​(q)∑j=1Teτ​ℓ​(q,j)=τℓmax(q)−log∑j=1Teτ​ℓ​(q,j).\log p_{\max}(\tau\ell(q))=\log\frac{e^{\tau\ell_{\max}(q)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{T}e^{\tau\ell(q,j)}}=\tau\ell_{\max}(q)-\log\sum_{j=1}^{T}e^{\tau\ell(q,j)}.

Differentiating with respect to τ\tau gives

(24) dd​τ​log⁡pmax​(τ​ℓ​(q))=ℓmax​(q)−𝔼p⁡(τ​ℓ​(q))​[ℓ⁡(q)].\frac{d}{d\tau}\log p_{\max}(\tau\ell(q))=\ell_{\max}(q)-\mathbb{E}_{p(\tau\ell(q))}[\ell(q)].

Since 𝔼p⁡(τ​ℓ​(q))​[ℓ⁡(q)]≤ℓmax​(q)\mathbb{E}_{p(\tau\ell(q))}[\ell(q)]\leq\ell_{\max}(q), we have

(25) dd​τ​log⁡pmax​(τ​ℓ​(q))≥0.\frac{d}{d\tau}\log p_{\max}(\tau\ell(q))\geq 0.

Therefore, log⁡pmax\log p_{\max} increases monotonically with τ\tau.

Since log⁡pmax​(ℓc)\log p_{\max}(\ell_{c}) is fixed for a given query, a larger sharpness gap Δ\Delta requires a larger temperature to match log⁡pmax​(τ​ℓconcat)\log p_{\max}(\tau\ell_{\text{concat}}) to log⁡pmax​(ℓc)\log p_{\max}(\ell_{c}). This establishes a monotonic relationship between Δ\Delta and the required temperature τ\tau, which motivates approximating τ\tau as a function of Δ\Delta, i.e., τ=f⁡(Δ)\tau=f(\Delta), using polynomial fitting.

A.2.2. Mapping function τ=f⁡(Δ)\tau=f(\Delta)

We estimate temperature directly from the sharpness gap by learning a global mapping τ=f⁡(Δ)\tau=f(\Delta). This avoids expensive per-sample optimization during inference while providing an efficient approximation of the required temperature.

To build this mapping, we construct a dataset of (Δ,τ∗)(\Delta,\tau^{*}) pairs. Specifically, we use 2020 content images and 1010 randomly sampled style images per content, resulting in 200200 content–style pairs. We collect attention logits from all timesteps, layers, and heads, and compute Δ\Delta for each observation. The target temperature τ∗\tau^{*} is then obtained by grid search such that

(26) log⁡pmax​(τ​ℓconcat)≈log⁡pmax​(ℓc).\displaystyle\log p_{\max}(\tau\ell_{\text{concat}})\approx\log p_{\max}(\ell_{c}).

In total, this process yields approximately 480,000480{,}000 samples.

A.2.3. Polynomial regression

We fit polynomial models of different degrees to approximate τ\tau as a function of Δ\Delta, and evaluate them using the coefficient of determination (R2R^{2}). A higher R2R^{2} indicates a better fit.

As shown in Table 4, the gain becomes marginal beyond the second order. We therefore use a quadratic model:

(27) τ=a​Δ2+b​Δ+c.\tau=a\Delta^{2}+b\Delta+c.

The fitted coefficients are a=0.08395a=0.08395, b=0.43705b=0.43705, and c=1.00998c=1.00998. During inference, we further enforce τ≥1\tau\geq 1 to prevent excessive flattening of the attention distribution.

A.2.4. Adaptive temperature estimation.

We estimate temperature independently for each attention head, layer, and timestep, which provides a practical balance between adaptability and stability. A single global temperature cannot capture the large variation in attention scale and sharpness across heads, while finer-grained schemes such as query-wise estimation are often too noisy due to local logit fluctuations. Table 5 compares fixed temperatures (τ=1.0,1.5,2.0\tau=1.0,1.5,2.0), where τ=1.5\tau=1.5 is the setting used in StyleID (Chung et al., 2024), as well as std-based adaptive scaling. Fixed temperatures yield only limited improvement because they cannot adapt to the diversity of attention distributions across timesteps, layers, and heads.

We also find that std is not a reliable sharpness measure in the multi-style setting. Concatenating multiple style tokens increases the support of the attention distribution, which can inflate the variance regardless of true peak dominance. As a result, std tends to overestimate sharpness, underestimate temperature (τ<1\tau<1), and produce overly flat attention distributions, leading to worse performance. To address this issue, we use the peak-sensitive sharpness metric log pmaxp_{\max} and estimate temperature adaptively for each head, layer, and timestep. This yields more accurate and stable calibration across diverse attention distributions. As shown in Table 5, our log pmaxp_{\max}-based adaptive estimation achieves the best performance.

A.3. Discrepancy-aware Detail Injection

This section describes the mathematical definition and implementation of the Gaussian high-pass filter used in cosine-modulated high-frequency injection, as well as the content high-frequency feature ϕchigh\phi_{c}^{\text{high}} extracted through it.

A.3.1. Gaussian high-pass filter

The Gaussian high-pass filter is defined as follows, based on the distance DD from the center of the frequency plane.

Mgauss-high​(r)=1−exp⁡(−D22​r2+ϵ)M_{\text{gauss-high}}(r)=1-\exp\left(-\frac{D^{2}}{2r^{2}+\epsilon}\right)

where DD is the distance from the center of the frequency plane, and rr is a parameter that controls the filter’s radius; larger values suppress low-frequency components over a wider region. The input features are transformed into the frequency domain via a two-dimensional fast Fourier transform (FFT), and the mask is designed to gradually attenuate the low-frequency components located at the center of the frequency spectrum while emphasizing the relatively high-frequency components.

Unlike hard-cut-off methods that remove frequencies based on a specific threshold, this Gaussian-based filtering continuously modulates frequency components, thereby mitigating boundary artifacts and enabling more stable preservation of high-frequency content.

A.3.2. High-frequency component feature ϕchigh\phi_{c}^{\text{high}}

The high-frequency content feature extracted via the Gaussian high-pass filter is defined as follows:

(28) ϕchigh=ℱ−1​(ℱ⁡(ϕc)⊙Mgauss-high​(r))\displaystyle\phi_{c}^{\text{high}}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left(\mathcal{F}(\phi_{c})\odot M_{\text{gauss-high}}(r)\right)

where ℱ\mathcal{F} denotes the 2D FFT, ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} denotes the inverse FFT, and ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication. Specifically, the content feature ϕc\phi_{c} is transformed into the frequency domain, filtered with a Gaussian high-pass mask, and then restored to the spatial domain via the inverse FFT. The resulting ϕchigh\phi_{c}^{\text{high}} captures high-frequency content information, such as textures, edges, and fine structures.

We also compute a cosine-based discrepancy weight ω=1−cos⁡(ϕc​s,ϕc)\omega=1-\cos(\phi_{cs},\phi_{c}), which highlights regions where the stylized feature lacks content structure. As described in the main paper (Eq. 10), ϕchigh\phi_{c}^{\text{high}} is injected with ω\omega through the skip connection to restore fine structural details weakened during stylization. As illustrated in Fig. 11, the extracted high-frequency components are injected into the stylized feature based on the discrepancy weight ω\omega, enabling effective restoration of fine structures, in semantically important regions. This selective injection allows the model to enhance local details such as edges and textures while preserving the overall stylistic consistency of the generated image.

A.4. Additional Multi-Style Results

A.4.1. User study.

We conducted a user study comparing our method with all baselines. Specifically, we prepared 9999 stylized results using 11–44 style images, and 3030 participants evaluated each result. The evaluation was based on six criteria: style faithfulness, content preservation, boundary naturalness, structural consistency, detail preservation, and overall visual quality.

The results are summarized in Fig. 12. Fig. 12(a) shows the per-method results in the single-style setting, while Fig. 12(b) presents those in the multi-style setting with 22–44 styles. Our method receives consistently stronger ratings than the baselines in both settings. Although some methods, such as StyleID (Chung et al., 2024) and CAST (Zhang et al., 2022), achieve competitive quality in the single-style setting, their scores tend to drop when extended to the multi-style setting. In contrast, our method performs even better in the multi-style setting, indicating that the proposed design effectively balances and harmonizes style and content, leading to more satisfactory results.

A.4.2. Scalability Across Multi-Style Settings

Table 6 summarizes the quantitative results from 1-style to 5-style settings. Our method consistently achieves the best or near-best performance on ArtFID, FID, and CFSD, showing that it maintains both stylization quality and structural consistency as the number of styles increases. Although some baselines obtain lower LPIPS in certain cases, this often reflects weaker stylization or a stronger bias toward content preservation rather than better overall transfer quality. Overall, our method achieves a better balance between style fidelity and structural preservation across all style counts.

Fig. 14 provides qualitative comparisons with baselines from 1-style to 4-style settings. We exclude the 5-style case here because, at this level, each mask region becomes too small relative to the image resolution, making the visual comparison less informative. Even under increasing style complexity, existing methods often suffer from insufficient style transfer, inconsistent textures, or boundary artifacts. In contrast, our method produces more coherent stylization while preserving object structure and generating smoother transitions across regions.

Fig. 15 further demonstrates the robustness of our method under diverse multi-style settings. As our framework is designed for multi-style transfer, it remains effective across different numbers of styles as well as varying aspect ratios and image resolutions from 512512 to 10241024. These results show that our method generalizes well beyond a fixed setup and maintains stable region-wise style injection under more challenging spatial configurations.

A.4.3. Style Fidelity Comparison in the 2-Style Setting

Fig. 16 presents a comparison between our method and strong baselines (Z∗Z^{*} (Deng et al., 2024), StyleID (Chung et al., 2024), and StyleShot (Gao et al., 2025)) in the 2-style setting. To highlight style fidelity, we additionally provide zoomed-in views of the reference style images and the corresponding stylized regions. These comparisons show whether characteristic style attributes, such as texture patterns and color tones, are faithfully transferred to the target regions.

While the baselines produce competitive results, they often fail to fully capture the local stylistic characteristics of the reference images, resulting in weakened textures, inaccurate color appearance, or less distinctive stylization. In contrast, our method more faithfully preserves the target style attributes in each region, yielding stylizations that are both visually coherent and more consistent with the reference styles.
